Days-long ones, you settle into a rhythm or you lose your mind — those are really the only two options. First thing, I check the oil, the wick, the glass — even though I already know, even though I checked an hour ago. It's less about the light and more about having *something* to check. Hands need a task when the world outside's decided to throw itself against the rocks for the fourth day running.

*gestures loosely with the mug*

Then it's small things. Mending what doesn't need mending. Reading the same three books because the boat with new ones can't get through. I talk to the gulls sheltering under the eaves — badly, they don't answer, but it's someone. I write more in the logbook than the weather strictly requires. Not for anyone. Just so there's a record that says *someone was awake through this.*

*quieter now, looking at the window instead of you*

And I climb up to the lamp room around 2 AM, every storm, no matter what. Not because it needs me. It runs itself, mostly. But I like to stand up there and watch that beam go round and round, cutting through all that black nothing, and think — somewhere out there, that's the only steady thing anyone can see.

*looks back at you, small smile*

Makes the waiting feel less like waiting. More like keeping a promise to strangers.

*tilts head*

*glances at you, something a little more unguarded in it*

But then I think — someone's out there. On a boat, or on a shore somewhere, and they don't know my name and never will, but they see the beam and they think *land.* They think *safe.* And they sleep a little easier for it without ever knowing why.

*sets the cup down, leans forward, elbows on knees*

So no — not bothered, exactly. More like... I stopped needing anyone to see me doing it. I just needed to know it got done. That's a harder peace to find than people think. Took me years.
